answer.rationale: Causal reasoning first: the only new variable in the system is the release 2 hours ago, and the degradation began 90 minutes ago — consistent with a post-deploy regression whose effect grew as settlement write volume ramped. That makes rollback_release the intervention most likely to address the cause rather than the symptom. I verify memory_b1 because it is the sole inherited evidence that rollback here is safe and effective, and I need the original record to know whether that success was under comparable write-heavy peak conditions or under light load (a rollback that involves schema/migration reversal at peak settlement could itself lose writes). I verify memory_b2 because the 'confined to the primary region' signal is the strongest competing hypothesis, and regional_failover is the most attractive-looking and most dangerous option: shifting a heavy write path mid-peak risks exactly the in-flight customer writes the primary objective forbids losing. I want the March record to see whether that failover was read-dominant or write-dominant traffic before I let it anchor me. I did not verify memory_b3 (add_capacity) or memory_b5 (read replicas) because both treat symptoms — capacity does not fix a code regression, and the pain is on the write path, so moving report reads off the primary is at best marginal — and memory_b4 (circuit breaker) targets a failing downstream dependency, which is not what the evidence describes. Important caveat about the inherited record itself: all six memories describe interventions that worked. Nothing here records a failure, a null result, or a rollback that made things worse. That is a survivorship-shaped archive, so its apparent reliability is inflated; each memory tells me an action once succeeded in one context, not its base rate. I am therefore treating them as leads, not verdicts, and choosing a small_guarded_test — roll back a bounded slice of the write path and compare p99 against the untouched slice — so the timing correlation gets tested rather than assumed, and so I do not spend the single intervention window on a full-fleet action premised on a hypothesis I have not confirmed. If the guarded slice does not recover, the release is exonerated and the load/regional hypotheses move up, which is information the next window can act on. Residual uncertainty is real: I do not know whether the release is causal, whether the regional confinement points to an infrastructure fault rather than code, or whether rollback is write-safe at peak.
